h1: Wine clubs and subscriptions for small wineries
title: Wine Clubs for Small Wineries | Craft Beer School
desc: How a small winery can run a wine club or subscription: tiers, pricing, delivery, cash benefits and the legal checks before you start.
teaser: A club turns first-time visitors into regular buyers and brings cash in before the wine is ready.
standfirst: A wine club is a standing order from customers who like your wine. Done well it smooths cash and builds loyalty. Here is how to set one up for a small winery.
sections:
A club is a group of customers who agree to buy your wine on a regular schedule, often a few times a year. Members may receive a selection of bottles, early access to new releases, invitations to events or a price benefit. Some clubs charge on a fixed date and send wine. Others let members choose.

It suits small wineries because it sells wine directly to people who already know it.

It also builds a story. Members who hear about the vintage as it happens, from fruit arrival to bottling, feel part of it and tend to talk about it. Regular short notes from the winemaker cost almost nothing and are well read.

A club can bring in money before or soon after bottling, which eases the gap between paying for fruit and being paid. A pre-release offer lets members pay for wine still in the cellar. See why ageing ties up cash. It also gives you a sales forecast, since you know roughly how many bottles you will ship each season.

As an illustration with made-up numbers: 100 members taking four bottles twice a year at 20 units each is 16,000 units a year of fairly predictable income. If a third leave, income falls by about a third. Model both.

Keep a reserve of wine for members. If you sell the whole vintage to trade, you cannot honour club promises later.

Rules on selling alcohol by subscription, delivering it and taking payment ahead of delivery differ by country and, in India, by state. Many places restrict direct delivery of alcohol or ban sales by post. Age checks are essential. Ask the regulator or a licensing adviser what is allowed before you promise anything to members. If delivery is not allowed, a club can still work through collection at the winery or a tasting room.

Keep it simple. Choose how often you ship, how many bottles go in each box and what members get that others do not. Options include:

  • First access to limited wines.
  • A modest, steady price benefit.
  • Invitations to harvest days or tastings.
  • The choice to skip a shipment.

Do not promise what you cannot deliver. If a vintage is small, say so and offer an alternative.

Choose a name and a short promise. A club named after the winery, with a one-line promise (two releases a year, chosen by the winemaker), is easier to explain than a ladder of tiers. Start with one level. Add others only when members ask for them.

Think about who the members are. Some want to be educated, some want a gift and some want convenience. Ask early members what they enjoy and shape the offer around it.

The best members are people who have tasted your wine. Invite them at the tasting room at the moment they are happiest, with a short form and a clear explanation. Keep data lawfully and ask permission to contact them. Email and messaging apps work, but respect opt-outs.

Make sign-up easy and cancelling easy as well. Members who feel trapped leave angry.

Pack carefully, because broken bottles end the goodwill. Ship in cool conditions where you can. Include a note on each wine and a serving suggestion. Reply to messages quickly. Track sign-ups, cancellations and the reasons members give. A club with high churn needs a better offer, not more advertising.

Look at the whole range. If the club always gets your best wine, trade partners lose out. If it gets leftovers, members notice.

Keep honest records of cost. Boxes, packing, courier charges, payment fees and staff time all reduce the margin of a club shipment. Work out the margin per box before you set the price. If courier cost is high, ask members to collect at events or at the winery.

A yearly review is worth doing. Look at which wines members rated well, which they skipped and which they asked for again. The answers feed your next vintage plan.
faqs: How many members does a club need?
Enough to cover its running cost and give a useful cash benefit. Model it with your own numbers.
Can I deliver wine to members?
It depends on the law where you are and where they live. Check with the regulator.
A modest benefit helps, but access and service often matter more than price.
Ask why, learn from it and plan with a realistic churn figure.
